title: Representational and Control Subdivisions

Ventrolateral prefrontal cortex in macaques guides decisions in different learning conditions; Working Memory as Programmable Fast Weight Computation

WM relies more on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, whereas maintaining information in mind but not manipulating it 3 does not need involvement of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (D’Esposito et al. 1999, Eldreth et al. 2006, Smith & Jonides 1999). Imaging studies show frontal activation only in ventrolateral prefrontal cortex for memory maintenance that is not suprathreshold. 4

A compact way to organize the system is: representational hubs encode long-horizon, amodal regularities; control circuits tune access, competition, and task alignment. On the representational side, a graded, transmodal core spans bilateral anterior/ventral temporal cortex, angular gyrus (ventral PGp), medial prefrontal cortex, and posterior cingulate/precuneus. These regions lie at the apex of the principal connectivity gradient and support content-rich, modality-invariant concepts and situation models that can be recombined across contexts.

By contrast, a left-leaning semantic control network (SCN) comes online when retrieval must be shaped to context, cues are weak, or competitors are strong. Meta-analyses and causal perturbations highlight left inferior frontal gyrus-subserving controlled retrieval in anterior/ventral BA45 and selection among competitors in more dorsal/posterior IFG/IFS-together with posterior middle/inferior temporal cortex, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex/pre-SMA, and dorsal parietal control zones (dorsal AG/IPS). These areas bias access to non-dominant associations, resolve competition, and reformat conceptual outputs into a task-appropriate code. Critically, pMTG sits at the anatomical "middle ground" between DMN and the multiple-demand (MD) executive system (which is implicated in domain-general control), coupling to ventral IFG during control-heavy semantic judgments and to IFS/IPS when selection demands rise-consistent with its role as a nexus linking representational hubs to control machinery 5, 6, 7.

The SCN is not a carbon copy of the MD network, nor is it simply an extension of the DMN. Topographic and connectivity analyses place it in an intermediate zone between the two, allowing it to dynamically recruit resources from either end of the cortex’s principal connectivity gradient 8, 9. When a task involves strong, well-learned associations, SCN activity shifts toward the transmodal end of the gradient-functionally coupling with DMN hubs like ATL, AG, and mPFC to exploit automatic, richly integrated representations. When the task instead demands retrieval of weak or novel associations, or selection of atypical features, SCN regions shift their coupling toward the sensory-coupled, executive-control end of the gradient-aligning more with MDN regions such as IFS and IPS to impose stronger top-down constraints. This ability to "flex along the principal gradient" means the SCN can reconfigure its network position to favor either automatic, knowledge-driven processing or effortful, control-driven processing as needed-a dynamic now directly observed in surface-based "informational connectivity" analyses during semantic search tasks.

Two cortical interfaces are particularly important. First, a language interface maps conceptual content to lexical and syntactic forms via a temporal-frontal pathway: mid/anterior STS-MTG and temporal pole support lexical-semantic access and combinatorics along a ventral stream, while left IFG parcels implement unification, selection, and morpho-syntactic operations; a complementary dorsal stream supports sensorimotor mappings for articulation. This architecture explains how the same conceptual representation can be verbalized under varying constraints, and why linguistic difficulty recruits adjacent MD control regions while core language regions remain functionally distinct 10, 11, 12. Second, a working-memory/attention interface recruits MDN (IFJ/IFS, dlPFC, IPS) proportionally to semantic processing difficulty, stabilizing intermediate goal states and sequencing multi-step inferences; in naturalistic tasks, language, DMN, and MDN remain dissociable yet coordinative, with MDN providing domain-general control that scaffolds semantic selection when demands escalate 13, 14.

Value and goals modulate semantic access via a vmPFC/OFC interface. vmPFC carries a domain-general subjective-value code that can weight candidate interpretations or inferences, while OFC represents a cognitive map of task/state space, supplying the currently relevant state features that semantic control should target. This arrangement links abstract knowledge to goal-directed behavior: vmPFC/OFC bias which meanings are worth pursuing and which features of the situation should be integrated next 15, 16, 17.

Subcortical partners close the loop. Pre-SMA/ACC interact with basal ganglia and mediodorsal thalamus to gate retrieval, update task sets, and broadcast the selected interpretation to cortical workspaces 18, 19, 20. Word-generation and semantic retrieval studies implicate a pre-SMA-caudate-anterior thalamic loop during access to stored lexical-semantic knowledge, while converging human and primate data assign MD thalamus a regulatory role in prefrontal-dependent cognition, including selection among lexical-semantic alternatives. These cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits provide the control dynamics-initiation, maintenance, and switching-that the cortical SCN exploits 21.

Putting this together: the representational core (ATL/ventral AG-PGp/mPFC/PCC) furnishes amodal, recombinable structure over long horizons; the SCN (LIFG/IFJ, pMTG/ITG, dmPFC/pre-SMA, dorsal AG/IPS) tunes entry into, traversal of, and readout from that structure to meet task goals; language and MDN interfaces render the content in communicable form and manage difficulty; and vmPFC/OFC plus fronto-striato-thalamic loops supply goal/value signals and control gating. This fractionation explains classic dissociations: representational damage (e.g., bilateral ATL degeneration) yields degraded knowledge across modalities, whereas control-network lesions ("semantic aphasia") spare stored content but produce context-inappropriate retrieval that is disproportionately impaired under weak cues or high competition.
